analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal to charge unconscionably excessive prices for essential goods during emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in March 2022 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal offense, enforced by the FTC, to sell essential goods or services at an unconscionably excessive price during or in anticipation of a natural disaster, pandemic, or declared state of emergency [S2][S3]. It defines the violation by comparing the emergency price to the ordinary price before the crisis [S3], requires the FTC to set up a hotline and website for people to report price gouging [S3], and leaves every state's own price-gouging law in place [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who need essentials during a crisis: people buying water, food, medicine, fuel, generators, or hotel rooms after a hurricane or during a pandemic. State attorneys general and the FTC also gain a federal backstop against sellers who raise prices to a gross disparity over pre-crisis levels [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to sell or offer essential goods or services at an unconscionably excessive price during, or in anticipation of, a natural disaster, pandemic, or declared state of emergency [S2][S3].
Defines the violation as a gross disparity between the crisis price and the ordinary pre-crisis price, and puts FTC enforcement powers behind it, including penalties under the FTC Act [S3].
Requires the FTC to operate a telephone hotline and online reporting tool for price-gouging complaints, active during a crisis and for 120 days after it ends [S3].
Explicitly leaves state price-gouging laws untouched, so stronger state protections still apply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers of essential goods and services, including large retailers, e-commerce platforms, fuel sellers, hotels, and online marketplace resellers, who could face FTC penalties for emergency price spikes that a court or the FTC found to be a gross disparity over ordinary prices. Honest sellers whose costs genuinely rose would have a defense, since the law targets unjustified increases [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Sellers of essential goods and services

drawbacks.text: The standard is vague: 'unconscionably excessive' and 'gross disparity' give the FTC and courts wide discretion, and some critics of federal price-gouging bans argue that high prices during shortages also ration scarce goods and signal suppliers to bring more in, so capping them can worsen shortages.
The bill would add federal enforcement on top of laws that most states already have, raising compliance questions for national retailers about which rules apply and adding FTC workload.
Because it applies even in anticipation of an emergency, sellers could face liability for price adjustments made before a crisis is formally declared.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: it protects people at their most vulnerable, when they cannot shop around for water, medicine, or fuel, and the biggest practical objection, that price caps can worsen shortages, is limited here because the ban applies only to essentials during a defined crisis rather than a general price control. The cost is modest enforcement complexity for businesses and a somewhat vague legal standard. On balance the bill would help consumers more than it would burden sellers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on March 15, 2022, joined by Senators Blumenthal, Cortez Masto, and Hirono [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
The committee took no further action, and no version of the bill ever received a vote in the Senate or the House before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers of essential goods, from national retail chains to online resellers, are better off because the bill never became law: they face no federal price-gouging penalties and remain subject only to whatever state laws apply.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a federal price-gouging ban enforced by the FTC.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal, Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, and Sen. Mazie Hirono

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or advanced it, so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Republican Conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but no vote was ever taken, so the bill's fate reflects committee inaction rather than a recorded partisan split [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Retailers and e-commerce sellers of essential goods
industries.note: The bill would expose them to FTC penalties for emergency price spikes on essentials like water, medicine, and fuel [S3]. Their financial interest in charging crisis prices runs against the consumers the bill protects.

Marketplace sellers who marked up masks, sanitizer, and generators during the pandemic would be the clearest targets of the 'gross disparity' standard, which reaches offers made even in anticipation of a crisis [S3].

industries.industry: Fuel sellers, hotels, and travel providers
industries.note: These businesses commonly raise prices around declared emergencies, exactly the conduct the bill would police, and the bill extends FTC jurisdiction to common carriers and nonprofits that the FTC normally cannot reach [S3].
The bill gives the FTC new authority, rulemaking power, and a public complaint hotline, expanding its consumer-protection mandate [S3].
